title_options: The Memo That Admitted Nokia Was on Fire
How Nokia Lost the Phone It Invented
From Paper Mill to Phone King to Footnote
Nokia Had 40% of the Market. Then 2007 Happened.
description:
In February 2011, the CEO of the world's biggest phone maker sent his staff a memo comparing the company to a burning oil platform.

This is the story of how Nokia went from a Finnish paper mill to owning the phone market, and how it lost all of it in a few years.

beats.narration: February 2011. A memo lands in the inboxes of Nokia employees around the world.
It's from the new CEO. And it says the company is standing on a burning platform.
Nokia was still the biggest phone maker on Earth. So how did it get here?
The story starts in 1865, with a mining engineer named Fredrik Idestam and a wood pulp mill in southern Finland.
The company took its name from the river nearby. Nokia.
By the late 2000s, roughly 40 percent of the phones sold worldwide carried the Nokia name.

visual.query: Nokia global market share, about 40% late 2000s

beats.narration: Then, in 2007, Apple walked on stage with a phone that was almost all screen.
Nokia's software, Symbian, was built for buttons. The world was moving to glass.

visual.query: close up of old keypad phone

beats.narration: Days after the memo, Nokia announced it would build its smartphones on Microsoft's Windows Phone.

visual.query: Nokia Microsoft Windows Phone partnership announcement February 2011

beats.narration: In September 2013, Microsoft announced it would buy the phone business outright. The deal closed in April 2014.

visual.query: Microsoft press release September 2013 Nokia acquisition

beats.narration: Nokia didn't vanish. It became something quieter: a company that builds the networks your phone runs on.

shorts.hook: Imagine getting this email from your CEO.
shorts.why: Self-contained tension with a question at the end

shorts.hook: Nokia owned 40% of the market. Then one phone showed up.
